cards.title: Safe Knife Use
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why a sharp knife is safer
- cut with the claw grip and a stable board
- carry, drop and store knives safely

cards.title: Almost every knife injury is avoidable
cards.body:
Knives are the most-used tool in any kitchen, and used well they are perfectly safe. But a moment's carelessness can cause a nasty cut that puts you out of action and leaves the team short.

Almost every knife injury can be avoided with a few simple habits.

items.title: One careless moment
items.text: A nasty cut and a short team.

cards.title: A sharp knife is the safer knife
cards.body:
It sounds backwards, but a sharp knife is safer than a blunt one. A sharp blade cuts cleanly with little pressure, whereas a blunt knife needs force and is far more likely to slip.

Use the right knife for the job, and cut on a stable, non-slip board.

cards.title: The claw grip
cards.body:
Curl your fingertips under and let your knuckles guide the blade. Always cut down and away from your body, never towards your hand.

Keep your eyes on what you are doing. This is not the moment for a chat over your shoulder.

cards.title: Carry, drop, store
cards.body:
Carry a knife point-down by your side, and warn people if you are moving through the kitchen.

Never leave a knife in a sink of water where someone could grab it by the blade, and never try to catch a falling knife: step back and let it drop, then pick it up. Wash and store knives safely as soon as you have finished with them.

left.title: Do
items: Step back and let a falling knife drop
Wash and store it straight after use

right.title: Do not
items: Leave a knife in a sink of water
Try to catch a falling knife
Chat over your shoulder while cutting

cards.title: Steady board, right knife
cards.body: If your chopping board is sliding around, pop a damp cloth underneath. Choose the right knife for the job before you start.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one
- Use the right knife on a stable, non-slip board
- Claw grip, and cut down and away from your body
- Carry point-down by your side, and never catch a falling knife
- Never leave a knife in a sink of water, and wash and store it straight away

cards.q: A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one.
cards.why: A sharp blade cuts cleanly with little pressure, whereas a blunt one needs force and is more likely to slip.

cards.q: Why is a blunt knife more dangerous?
options: It needs more force and slips more
It is heavier in the hand
It cuts too cleanly to feel
cards.why: A blunt knife needs force and is far more likely to slip.
Curl your fingertips under and let your knuckles guide the blade.

cards.q: You should cut down and away from your body.
cards.why: Always cut down and away from your body, never towards your hand.

cards.q: A knife falls off the bench. What should you do?
options: Step back and let it fall
cards.why: Never try to catch a falling knife. Step back, let it drop, then pick it up.

cards.q: It is okay to leave a knife in a sink full of water for a moment.
cards.why: Someone could grab it by the blade. Wash and store knives safely as soon as you have finished.

cards.q: How should you carry a knife when walking through the kitchen?
cards.why: Carry a knife point-down by your side, and warn people if you are moving through the kitchen.

cards.q: Your chopping board is sliding around. What should you do?
options: Put a damp cloth under it
Hold it with your blade hand
cards.why: Cut on a stable, non-slip board. A damp cloth underneath stops it sliding.

cards.q: Using the correct knife for the job helps keep you safe.
cards.why: Always use the right knife for the job.

cards.q: What should you do with a knife as soon as you have finished using it?
options: Leave it to soak in the sink
Pass it to the next cook
cards.why: Wash and store knives safely as soon as you have finished with them.
